Internal engineering memo: whether to buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of what we own

Recommendation up front: do not make a large hardware purchase yet. Run a focused utilisation and latency programme for the next two quarters, then buy only the capacity that remains demonstrably short after scheduling, batching, model routing, and workload shaping. If the evidence shows a durable gap, purchase a modest, reversible increment rather than a fleet. The decision is not “buy versus do nothing”; it is “buy now versus buy later with better information.”

The case for buying more hardware is understandable. Local inference is attractive because it keeps data inside our boundary, avoids per-token cloud pricing, and can give predictable latency for latency-sensitive products. If demand is growing, waiting feels like leaving money on the table. But the current numbers do not yet prove that the bottleneck is silicon. They show a mix of idle accelerators, bursty queues, oversized models for simple tasks, and workloads that are not being routed to the right tier. Buying more GPUs into that system would mostly increase idle capacity, power draw, maintenance load, and the chance that we pay for peak capacity while average utilisation stays low.

Cost is not only the sticker price. It includes depreciation, cooling, power, rack space, spare parts, staff time, security review, and the opportunity cost of engineering attention. Every week spent on procurement and installation is a week not spent on evaluation, observability, and product work. Cloud bursting is not free either, but it is elastic and reversible; owned hardware is cheaper at steady high utilisation and much worse at low or unpredictable utilisation. The right comparison is not “local versus cloud” in the abstract but “local plus cloud overflow versus more local capacity,” using our actual workload shape.

Latency deserves special care. Some products need tight p95 and p99 response times, and local inference may be the right answer for those paths. But latency is often dominated by queueing, model size, batching policy, and retrieval or preprocessing steps, not by the raw number of accelerators. A well-tuned queue with a smaller model can beat a larger model on an idle machine. We should instrument end-to-end latency, time-to-first-token, queue wait, cache hit rate, and failure recovery time before committing capital.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware can improve redundancy, but only if it is deployed with health checks, failover, and tested recovery paths. Otherwise it adds failure modes. Existing systems may already be reliable enough for most traffic if we fix noisy neighbours, isolate tenants, and cap batch sizes. For critical paths, redundancy matters; for batch analytics, throughput and cost matter more. We should classify workloads by criticality rather than treating all AI traffic as equally urgent.

Opportunity cost is the strongest argument for patience. The team is small. A large purchase would consume procurement, integration, and operations capacity at exactly the moment we need to improve evaluation quality and product reliability. That is not a reason to avoid hardware forever; it is a reason to sequence it.

Reversibility favours a staged approach. Cloud capacity can be turned up or down quickly. Leases and reserved instances are intermediate. Owned hardware is the least reversible and should be reserved for workloads with stable, high, predictable demand. If we buy, prefer modular capacity, avoid long lock-in, and keep a cloud overflow path.

Uncertainty is real. Demand may accelerate, models may become larger, or regulation may force more local processing. If utilisation after optimisation remains above a clear threshold, say sustained high utilisation with queueing delay and p95 latency above target, then a purchase is justified. If utilisation is low and latency is mostly queueing or model mismatch, the purchase would be premature.

So: fund a utilisation programme now, set a decision gate in two quarters, and buy only the proven shortfall. That is the most economical, reversible path, and it preserves the option to expand when the evidence is stronger.

To: Engineering leadership  
From: Infrastructure review  
Re: Buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of what we own  
Date: internal planning draft  

Recommendation up front: do not commit a large hardware purchase yet. Run a disciplined utilisation and latency program for the next 90 days, instrument the workloads honestly, and buy only the increment that remains after the obvious waste is removed. If the evidence shows sustained high utilisation, queueing, and p95 latency misses, then a phased purchase is justified. If it does not, the money is better spent on software, scheduling, and staffing.

The case for buying more hardware is understandable. Local capacity can reduce dependence on external services, improve predictability for latency-sensitive paths, keep sensitive data inside our boundary, and give the team a sense of control. For workloads with stable demand, strict residency requirements, or tight tail-latency budgets, owned accelerators can be cheaper over a multi-year horizon than repeated external calls. There is also a morale benefit: a team that owns its compute tends to understand its constraints better.

But the current evidence does not yet justify a broad expansion. The first question is not “how much hardware do we need?” but “what are the workloads actually doing?” Many AI deployments look expensive because they are idle most of the time, oversized for peak bursts, or poorly separated by priority. A model that is loaded for a long-running batch job may sit unused while a latency-sensitive request waits behind it. A GPU that is technically available may still be unavailable in practice because of memory fragmentation, queueing, or a scheduler that treats all jobs as equal. Buying more hardware into that environment can increase utilization only slightly while increasing power, cooling, maintenance, and operational risk.

Cost should be evaluated as total cost of ownership, not purchase price. Local hardware carries depreciation, power, cooling, spare parts, monitoring, security patching, driver upgrades, and the opportunity cost of engineers spending time on infrastructure instead of product. It also carries a hidden cost: the need to staff and retain people who understand accelerator behavior, networking, and failure modes. That is a real constraint for a small team. External capacity is more expensive per unit in some cases, but it is elastic, observable, and easier to stop. Leased or reserved capacity sits between the two and may be the right middle path.

Latency deserves special attention. If the pain is p95 or p99 delay, the fix may be routing, batching, caching, smaller models, speculative decoding, or separating interactive traffic from offline training. If the pain is throughput, then more accelerators may help. If the pain is reliability, then the issue may be redundancy, failover, and observability rather than raw capacity. Buying hardware without diagnosing which of these is failing can make the system faster in the lab and worse in production.

Reliability cuts both ways. Owned hardware can reduce external dependency, but it concentrates risk in our own racks, power feeds, and maintenance windows. External services can fail too, but they are often designed for scale and have mature failure handling. The right answer depends on whether our failures are caused by capacity, by external dependency, or by our own operational discipline.

Opportunity cost is the strongest argument for patience. Every week spent provisioning and tuning hardware is a week not spent improving the product, the evaluation harness, or the data pipeline. A small team should be skeptical of any large capital commitment that does not clearly move a product metric. At the same time, delay is not free: if users are already waiting, or if a launch is blocked by capacity, waiting too long has its own cost.

Reversibility matters. Software changes are cheap to reverse. Hardware purchases are not. A lease, reserved instance, or cloud burst path can be adjusted as demand changes. A purchased rack can be resold, but only with loss and delay. That asymmetry favors starting with reversible options.

Uncertainty is real. Demand may grow faster than expected, models may become larger, or latency requirements may tighten. We should not pretend the 90-day window will settle everything. But it can reveal whether the bottleneck is genuinely compute, or whether it is scheduling, model choice, or measurement.

So the decision is: instrument first, optimize second, buy third. Track utilization, queue depth, p95 latency, failure rate, cost per request, and the fraction of time each workload is actually active. Separate interactive from batch traffic. Add caching and model routing. Then revisit the purchase with data. If sustained utilization is high, latency remains poor, and the workload is stable, buy a modest increment and prefer leased or reserved capacity where possible. If utilization is low and latency is manageable, do not buy. The best hardware decision is the one that is not needed.

appliance.competing_traffic: none (sq27-test stopped; a stale sglang benchmark from 11-04 stopped with the operator's approval)
appliance.drafter: DSpark (bundled mtp.safetensors), 7 draft tokens, greedy drafts; speculation with one live request (ATLAS_DFLASH_BATCH_DEPTH=1:7,1000000:0) and only while drafts pay (ATLAS_DFLASH_ADAPTIVE=1: under 2 accepted a step over 12 steps decodes plainly until a re-probe 256 tokens later)
appliance.quantisation: Spark: calibrated GPTQ NVFP4 attention, lm_head and L20-23 experts over the shipped checkpoint, for decode and verify rows; prefill reads the checkpoint's own tensors, its experts' inputs quantized as its hf_quant_config.json requires (NVFP4 / MXFP8 rows, W4A4 / W8A8)
appliance.scheduler: SparkInkling default profile: max-num-seqs 8, gpu-memory-utilization 0.80, prefill chunks 4096, CUDA graphs, programmatic dependent launch (ATLAS_INKLING2_PDL=1), prefix caching with conv-state snapshots (--enable-prefix-caching, --ssm-cache-slots=128, ATLAS_QWEN4EXP_AUX_PINNED=1), --request-timeout=3600, --tool-max-tokens=32768
